change one’s mind verb

also change your mind, I’ve changed my mind, have second thoughts, change of heart, on second thought, on second thoughts

classical

Cic. Mur. 61: sententiam mūtāre numquam (Lewis & Short s.v. mūtō)
Traupman 289
Traupman 346

sententiam mūtāre

change one’s mind, change one’s opinion

Other words

  • cōnsilium mūtāre — change one’s plan, change one’s mind (about what to do)

    also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 4.4.4: ego rogātus mūtāvī cōnsilium meum (Lewis & Short s.v. mūtō)

    Sententia is what one thinks, cōnsilium what one means to do: changing one’s mind about going is cōnsilium mūtāre.

  • mentem mūtāre — change one’s attitude, one’s disposition

    also used · classical · Cic. Prov. Cons. 25: mentēs vestrās voluntātēsque (with mūtāre; Lewis & Short s.v. mūtō); Traupman 104: to change one’s mind, mentem mūtāre

    Traupman’s phrase. Cicero uses it of changing people’s disposition and feelings; for a change of opinion or of plan, sententiam or cōnsilium mūtāre is the usual phrase.

  • recōgitō, recōgitāre, recōgitāvī — think it over again

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Capt. prol. 51: homunculī quantī sunt, quom recōgitō! (Lewis & Short); Traupman 393

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.; in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra)

    Traupman gives cum ego recōgitō for “on second thought”, literally “when I think it over”. Lewis & Short calls the verb rare: Plautus several times, Cicero once (Q. Fr. 2.2.1).

Examples

  • animī mūtātiō

    a change of heartTraupman 289

  • cum ego recōgitō

    on second thoughtTraupman 393

See also decide, opinion, change.

SourcesLewis & Short: muto · Lewis & Short: sententia · Lewis & Short: consilium
